## Solution

Place $O$ at the origin with $OX$ along the positive $x$-axis and $OY$ along the positive $y$-axis. Then $P=(\cos\frac{\pi}{6},\sin\frac{\pi}{6})$.

Let the line $MN$ have unit normal $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ with $\alpha\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2})$. Its distance from $O$ is $d$, and since $P$ lies on it,
$$d=\cos\left(\alpha-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right).$$
The intercepts are $OM=\dfrac{d}{\cos\alpha}$, $ON=\dfrac{d}{\sin\alpha}$, and $MN=\dfrac{d}{\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}$.

So
$$OM+ON-MN=\frac{d(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha-1)}{\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}.$$
With $s=\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha$, we have $\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=\frac{s^2-1}{2}$, which gives
$$OM+ON-MN=\frac{2d}{1+s}=\frac{2\cos\left(\alpha-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)}{1+\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha}.$$

**Maximizing.** Set $\beta=\alpha-\frac{\pi}{6}$. Setting the derivative to zero and simplifying gives
$$\sin\beta=-\sqrt2\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{12}=-\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2},$$
so $\cos\beta=\sqrt{\sqrt3/2}$. This gives $\alpha\approx 8.5^\circ$, which is interior.

Using $\sin\alpha=\sin(\beta+\frac{\pi}{6})$ and $\cos\alpha=\cos(\beta+\frac{\pi}{6})$, the expression becomes
$$\frac{4c}{\sqrt3+(1+\sqrt3)c},\qquad c=\cos\beta.$$
Since $c^2=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, we have $\frac{\sqrt3}{c}=2c$, so the reciprocal simplifies to
$$\frac{1}{\text{value}}=\frac{1+\sqrt3+2c}{4},\qquad 2c=\sqrt{2\sqrt3}.$$

Hence the maximum is
$$\frac{4}{1+\sqrt3+\sqrt{2\sqrt3}}\approx 0.8709.$$

**Check.** The endpoints give $\alpha\to0$: $\approx0.866$, and $\alpha\to\frac{\pi}{2}$: $0.5$. Both are below the interior value. Numerical evaluation near $\alpha=8^\circ$–$9^\circ$ agrees with $0.8709$.

ANSWER: $\dfrac{4}{1+\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2\sqrt{3}}}$
